chapter: Touring and race on the road
title: Stranded on the road and the Thomasville, Georgia trouble
summary: Passing for white, wives mistaken for prostitutes, and robbery in Thomasville where a gas attendant trusted him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, of course, now all of my music life wasn't beautiful, I'll say. We really ran into some grave problems. I think I talked to you about some of these incidents a couple of times before. Being as light as I was, they considered me a white musician. Then when they found out that I was actually a Negro, then it changed the whole picture. Traveling with the wives in the bands, you ran into problems there with the police, thinking that they were prostitutes or something like that. And there was always some incidents coming up to put a block into your happiness, I'd say. But, of course, we always managed to smile at it after it was over with. And we were stranded a lot of times on the highways with nothing to eat, nothing to drink. And fortune would shine on us, somebody would come along and help us out. So we made it through the storm a lot of times that way.
You got stranded with no money, no nothing?

Right, right. Right. Right. Right. When we had this big trouble in Thomasville, Georgia, and I wanted to lynch the whole band, it took all of the money. We had made $150 that night, which was a lot of money for my band. Well, they took every dime we had. And got ready to get the gas to go to Macon, Georgia, which was 150 miles. The attendant was a good enough man to give me enough gas and trust me with gas and oil to get to Macon, Georgia. Then I sent him his money for Macon as soon as I got there. I knew the doctor that was promoting the dancing. I wanted him his money right back. That's one of the many, many instances where you say everybody in this world is not bad. And you can't say that every white man is bad because it's a lie. You can't say every Negro is bad. It's a lie because everybody is not. Now this one particular fella, supposing he hadn't come to our aid, he'd probably been in the neck and jaw, I mean, in the east of the town of Thomasville, Georgia, dead now. And then of course the problems of eating on the highway, sleeping, and those accommodations, which today, like I explained in one of my talks to one of these singers at the Sabarell Center, I don't remember, I don't think you'll recall that television shot I made over here. They were playing here at the Brewer Room and I told a lady, I said, you could sit here and smile and enjoy what you're doing today. I said, it's beautiful. I said, but let me tell you some of the experiences that I've had to make it possible for you to enjoy this life today and see how hard it was. But these today, they don't know it. They don't know anything about the past. They're not looking for the past. They're looking for the present. And that's what it is. But I do think that history should be there and someone with a vivid idea and a memory of what happened in the early 20s, and the early 30s, would document this and document it correctly and don't pull any punches. Maybe out of a hundred, maybe ten might read it. But that is a fact there before your eyes would actually happen.

If you don't have any history and you don't have any tradition, then you're along with stuff. You know, they give you some sort of guide to how to behave. Well, of course, kids think they know it all. Anyhow, let me know if you want any coffee or anything.
Well, no, I'd rather finish this than drink to call it.
